newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Feb 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Feb 27.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Prepared for Reuters by The
Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- PACE OUSTS CO-FOUNDER AS IT WARNS AGAIN ON PROFITS

Pace Micro Technology has issued its second profits warning in three weeks. At the same time the company announced that co- founder Barry Rubery had left the board. Pace's non-executive chairman Peter Morgan said that Mr Rubery's management style was not compatible with that of a public company but denied that his departure was linked to the profits warning.
-- OPEN SKIES DEAL MAY BE ON HOLD UNTIL ELECTION

Discussions between the UK and the US on an open skies agreement are unlikely to be concluded until after the general election. An agreement is required before American officials will give the go-ahead to a proposed alliance between British Airways and American Airlines. The alliance may also include Japan Airlines, a prospect which is unwelcome to other airlines who fear it will lead to the formation of an "iron triangle" dominating air traffic in the US, Europe and Asia.
-- INVESTORS BACK OFF BETTING ON EMU

A survey published earlier this week by US investment bank Lehman Brothers has confirmed suspicions that international financial markets are concerned about a possible postponement of European Monetary Union (Emu). Lehman surveyed 38 international bond investors and found there has been a significant reduction of holdings in the 'peripheral' European markets which have most to gain from first round membership of Emu. Instead, investors are shifting the balance of their portfolios in favour of more secure markets such as Germany, Austria and the Netherlands.
-- BROWN REVEALS DETAILS OF BANK REFORM PROPOSALS
Gordon Brown, the shadow chancellor, has unveiled a series of

proposed reforms which would prepare the way for the eventual transfer of control over interest rate decisions away from the Treasury and into the hands of the Bank of England. Among the proposals, which Brown sees as a way of moving forward the process of reforming the system governing interest rates, are plans to replace the current panel of independent forecasters with a Council of Economic Advisers which would encompass a wider range of economic expertise.
-- INSTITUTIONS PRESS LABOUR ON WINDFALL TAX

The National Association of Pension Funds, the body which represents Britain's pension funds, is to seek talks with the Labour party over the windfall tax it proposes to levy on the privatized utilities should it win the forthcoming general election. The Association, which represents institutions which hold 35 per cent of all UK shares, says it intends to try to dissuade Labour from proceeding with the tax. Graham Allen, chairman of the NAPF's investment committee, told the Financial Times that the group is concerned about the principle of retrospective legislation.
-- BAe CALLS FOR HEADHUNTERS TO BE USED BY AIRBUS

British Aerospace is asking its partners in Airbus Industrie to appoint headhunters to seek new senior executives. BAe's chief executive Sir Richard Evans wants to ensure that the current practice of appointing Airbus executives on the basis of nationality does not continue when the consortium, comprising BAe, Aerospaciale of France, Daimler Benz Aerospace of Germany and Casa of Spain, is turned into a limited company.
-- BARCLAYS FALTERS IN 300 MILLION STERLING BUYBACK

On Wednesday morning Barclays Bank launched a 300 million sterling scheme to buy back its own shares. This follows the government's scrapping of tax repayment for buybacks last October. However by Wednesday afternoon the bank had only succeeded in buying back 9.2 million out of 26 million ordinary shares.
-- CASH RICH BAe SEES ORDERS MOUNT UP

British Aerospace has seen a surge in its order book from 6 billion sterling to 19.4 billion sterling. The company has won orders from the Ministry of Defence for Nimrod 2000 patrol aircraft and Storm Shadow missiles. Recently agreed orders from Australia and Quatar for Hawk advanced jet trainers are not included in the final order total. Meanwhile BAe, who have announced a 38 per cent rise in profits before tax and exceptional items, have been playing down speculation about a merger with GEC.
-- PRU RULES OUT EARLY SOCIETY BUY

Insurance giants Prudential have announced a 14 per cent rise in operating profits from continuing operations and ruled out any early acquisition of a UK building society. Prudential's chief executive Sir Peter Davis said that the group, which is currently bidding for mutual life insurance company Scottish Amicable, is still interested in building societies but prices
are too expensive at the present time.
-- INVESTMENT AND STERLING DIM LOGICA

The computing services group Logica reported an 18 per cent rise in pre tax profits for the six months to December 31st. This was at the top end of market expectations but lower than they might have been if not for investment in new UK activities and the strength of sterling. Logica's international side is growing strongly but this was partly offset by a decline in their traditional markets of government, space and transport.
